items.followUp: Define an enzyme and describe how it converts a substrate into products.

rubric.why: Enzymes act as biological catalysts and speed up chemical reactions.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for identifying enzymes as biological catalysts or stating that they speed up chemical reactions.

rubric.why: A substrate with a suitable shape binds to the enzyme's specific active site.
rubric.description: Describes substrate binding at the active site.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for stating that the substrate binds at a suitable or specific active site.

rubric.why: Binding of the substrate to the enzyme forms an enzyme-substrate complex.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for stating that binding forms an enzyme-substrate complex.

rubric.why: Products are released, and the enzyme remains unchanged and can be used again.
rubric.description: Explains product release and enzyme reuse.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for stating that products are formed and released, and 1 mark for stating that the enzyme remains unchanged or can be reused.

modelAnswer: Enzymes are biological catalysts, usually proteins, that speed up chemical reactions in living organisms.
A substrate with a suitable shape binds to the enzyme's specific active site.
This binding forms an enzyme substrate complex.
The substrate is converted into products, which are released from the active site.
The enzyme remains unchanged and can be used again.

items.followUp: Describe how light intensity, carbon dioxide concentration and temperature affect the rate of photosynthesis.

rubric.why: A limiting factor restricts photosynthesis when it is in short supply or at an unsuitable level.
rubric.description: Explains what a limiting factor is.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for explaining that a limiting factor restricts the rate because it is in short supply or at an unsuitable level.

rubric.why: Increasing light intensity raises the rate until another factor becomes limiting.
rubric.description: Explains the effect of light intensity.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for linking increased light intensity to an increased rate, usually until another factor limits it.

rubric.why: Carbon dioxide is used in photosynthesis, and more of it can increase the rate.
rubric.description: Explains the effect of carbon dioxide.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for stating that increasing carbon dioxide availability can increase the rate of photosynthesis.

rubric.why: The rate rises with temperature up to an optimum; excessive heat can damage enzymes and reduce the rate.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for describing the optimum temperature effect and the effect of excessive heat on enzymes or the rate.

modelAnswer: The rate of photosynthesis is limited by factors that are in short supply or at unsuitable levels.
As light intensity increases, the rate usually increases until another factor becomes limiting.
Increasing carbon dioxide concentration can increase the rate because carbon dioxide is used in photosynthesis.
Increasing temperature raises the rate up to an optimum; excessive temperature can damage enzymes and reduce the rate.

items.followUp: Explain how guard cells cause stomata to open and close.

rubric.why: Guard cells surround and control the opening and closing of each stoma.
rubric.description: Identifies the guard cells and their role.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for stating that guard cells surround or control the stoma.

rubric.why: In light, guard cells take up water by osmosis and become turgid.
rubric.description: Explains the change in guard cells associated with opening.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for linking water uptake with guard cells becoming turgid.

rubric.why: Turgid guard cells bend apart and open the stoma.
rubric.description: Explains how turgid guard cells open the stoma.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for linking turgid guard cells with the stoma opening.

rubric.why: When guard cells lose water, they become flaccid and the stoma closes.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for linking water loss and flaccidity in guard cells with closure of the stoma.

modelAnswer: Each stoma is surrounded by two guard cells that control its opening and closing.
In light, guard cells take up water by osmosis and become turgid.
The turgid guard cells bend apart, so the stoma opens.
When guard cells lose water, they become flaccid and the stoma closes; this commonly occurs in darkness.

items.followUp: Differentiate between a plant's root and flower in terms of their functions.

rubric.why: Roots, stems and leaves are vegetative organs.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for naming roots, stems and leaves as vegetative organs.

rubric.why: Flowers and related structures are involved in plant reproduction and the formation of fruits and seeds.
rubric.description: Identifies reproductive organs and their function.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for naming flowers or reproductive organs and linking them to reproduction.

modelAnswer: Vegetative organs include roots, stems and leaves; they perform functions such as absorption, support and food-making for plant growth.
Reproductive organs include flowers and the structures that form fruits and seeds; they take part in reproduction.

items.followUp: Define bioinformatics and name one type of biological information it can analyse.

rubric.why: Bioinformatics uses computers and information technology to work with biological information.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for linking the use of computers with biological information.

rubric.why: DNA and protein sequences are examples of biological information analysed using bioinformatics.
rubric.description: Gives an example of information analysed.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for naming DNA sequences or protein sequences as data that bioinformatics can analyse.

modelAnswer: Bioinformatics is the use of computers and information technology to collect, store and analyse biological information.
It can be used to analyse DNA or protein sequences.
